verdicts.question: How many dry waste collection centres (DWCCs) operate in Bengaluru today (figures range from 119 in Sep 2025 to 164/166), who runs them and under what contracts with the city?
verdicts.problems: Verification limits first: no web source could be opened or searched in this session (the WebSearch budget was already exhausted at 200/200 before this sceptic pass, and page fetches are refused by the network policy), so nothing below is confirmed by a snippet; the checks are arithmetic, internal consistency, and independent research passes saved in the repo (docs/plan/research/answers/*.json and handoff/briefs-raw/*). (1) A factual error: the answer says the '164' figure 'could not be traced to any dated page', but two independent repo passes (kabadiwala-economics cluster and the public-systems brief) trace 164 DWCCs to Citizen Matters, 'Poor segregation is choking Bengaluru's waste system', 4 Nov 2025 — a later dated count than the 119 of 15 Sep 2025. So the newest published figure is 164 (Nov 2025), not 119, and the two probably differ on 'existing' vs 'operational'; the 'roughly 120' decision should say that. (2) Arithmetic does not reconcile: Rs 9.41 crore owed across 46 wards for '980 centre-months' is about Rs 96,000 per centre-month, roughly three times the stated MoU rate (Rs 56,316 per six months plus Rs 23,316 a month is about Rs 32,700 a month, i.e. 980 centre-months would be about Rs 3.2 crore). Either the dues cover other heads (vehicles, wages) or one figure is misread; not confirmed by snippet. (3) Figures found only in this cluster and confirmed by no other pass: 'more than 160' and '30-35 run efficiently' (Deccan Herald 11 Jan 2025), the 336 map pins, the MoU amounts, the operating-procedure terms (five categories, daily weights on BBMP portal, free drop of low-value waste, 'zero subsidies'), and '1,925 tonnes of dry waste a day, 1,200 processed (Aug 2025)', which has no source of that date in the list (other repo passes put dry waste at about 1,300-2,000 t/day, so the order of magnitude is plausible). (4) Corroborated by independent repo passes: 198 sanctioned, 141 remain, 119 operate, 127 wards, Hasiru Dala supports 35 (Citizen Matters 15 Sep 2025, also recorded by the identity, kabadiwala-economics and personas passes); Hasiru Dala's own Annual Report 2024-25 says 34 operator-run centres took in 19,811 t (about 54 t/day, 1.6 t/day per centre), which squares with '35'; the 369-ward GBA denominator (Citizen Matters 17 Sep 2026, in the handoff source list) and 119/369 = 32% ('about a third') is right; the UDD order of 2 Sep 2025 constituting five corporations is on BSWML's government-orders page. (5) Missed developments: the Solid Waste Management Rules 2026 (S.O. 388(E), 27 Jan 2026, in force 1 Apr 2026) make every 'entity involved in sorting of waste ... at Material Recovery Facility' register with the city corporation, report quarterly on the central portal and deal only with registered entities (rule 9), which covers DWCCs and any pilot yard; and BSWML's April 2026 Authorised Waste Processor list (five AWPs by corporation, Swachh Eco Solutions 'for dry waste only', Sustainable Impacts with Hasirudala Innovations for South) now channels bulk generators' dry waste through AWPs, not only DWCCs. Both are in the swm-2026 cluster and absent here. (6) Refined-chain conflict: the decision to treat each DWCC as a 'yard' node contradicts the founder's 30 Sep 2026 model, where 'Dry-waste centre / MRF' is its own role (city-agreement holder that buys loose sorted material from kabadiwalas, Saathis and bulk generators, outputs graded bales, and whose daily weight sheet and sale register Luma digitises), distinct from the Yard/Aggregator that bales for pre-processors.
verdicts.correction: Bengaluru's DWCC count has two dated public figures: 119 operational of 141 remaining (198 sanctioned) on 15 Sep 2025, and 164 on 4 Nov 2025 (both Citizen Matters); treat 164 as the newest 'existing' count and about 120 as the working 'functional' count, and confirm the pilot wards' list with the corporation's SWM wing. The 166 figure is May 2019. Operators are NGOs, waste-picker SHGs and individual waste-picker entrepreneurs (Hasiru Dala's own 2024-25 report counts 34 operator-run centres, about 1.6 t/day each, with only 31% of intake going to recyclers and the rest multilayer plastic and rejects); BBMP-era MoUs have lapsed and no city money flows, but the exact MoU amounts, the Rs 9.41 crore dues and the operating-procedure terms could not be re-verified and the dues figure does not reconcile with the stated rates, so keep them as 'reported, unconfirmed'. Two 2026 changes must be added: under SWM Rules 2026 rule 9 a DWCC or yard that sorts is a registrable MRF entity with quarterly portal reporting and a duty to deal only with registered parties (in force 1 Apr 2026; CPCB's portal had no MRF self-registration module as of 29 Sep 2026), and BSWML's 2026 Authorised Waste Processor list routes bulk-generator dry waste through five AWPs by corporation. In the refined chain model the DWCC is its own role, not a yard: it receives S1 (collected) material at an L1-type door price from Saathis, kabadiwalas and bulk generators (including zero-price low-value drops from the collection contractor), produces S2 sorted and S3 baled lots with a processing record whose yield and residual-waste share (about 31% saleable at Hasiru Dala centres) are recorded, and sells at L2/L3 to a yard or pre-processor; its daily weight sheet and sale register are the legal records Luma.Green keeps. Status: partly.

verdicts.question: Does the NAMASTE waste-picker component continue beyond FY2025-26, which resource organisation is empanelled for Karnataka, and has waste-picker registration started in Bengaluru?
verdicts.problems: Verification limits: no web source could be opened or searched in this session (WebSearch budget already exhausted at 200/200; fetches refused), so no claim is confirmed by a snippet; checks are internal consistency and independent repo passes. Corroborated independently: the scheme terms (SFC approval 20 Jun 2024 for FY2024-25 and 2025-26, Rs 250 per e-KYC-validated waste picker, Rs 10,000 per DWCC per month for 12 months, up to Rs 5 lakh per DWCC for vehicles, 750 DWCCs, scrap-sale receipts or scrap-shop endorsement as proof of occupation) are recorded by the public-systems brief and the identity cluster from the original 2024 guidelines PDF (socialjustice.gov.in/public/ckeditor/upload/86351727949710.pdf) and a namastescheme.com copy; the Bengaluru ID-card situation (BBMP cards expired, no new cards, about 10,437 issued through Hasiru Dala since 2011) is recorded by the identity cluster from the same Citizen Matters article. Not confirmed by any snippet or other pass: that a 'Revised' guideline PDF dated 15 Dec 2025 exists at the cited URL (other passes found only the 2024 original at a different URL), that the incentive was 'raised from Rs 150', the Rs 349.70 crore outlay (PIB 25 Aug 2023; note the commonly reported figure is Rs 349.73 crore, so check the last digit), the 2.34 lakh (17 Mar 2026), 2,51,756 (22 Sep 2026), 300+ cards in Delhi (4 Sep 2026) and Rs 498.73 crore rural-expansion figures, all of which come from secondary news or exam-prep sites rather than PIB or a Lok Sabha answer, and the portal dashboard figures (11 ROs, 10,894 profiles). Minor discrepancy: this answer dates the 1.52 lakh figure to 23 Jan 2026, while the identity cluster records it as a Parliament reply of 3 Feb 2026 (both via exam-prep sites). The progression 37,980 (Aug 2025) to 1.52 lakh to 2.34 lakh to 2,51,756 (Sep 2026) is monotonic and passes the 2.5 lakh target, so it is internally consistent. Missed development: SWM Rules 2026 rule 39(53) requires each ULB to keep a ward-wise database of informal waste collectors on the central portal (swm-2026 cluster), a second registration route for Saathis that the answer should mention alongside the NAMASTE ID. Refined-chain fit: the founder's roles file already gives the Saathi 'NAMASTE ID + scrap-sale receipts as proof of occupation' and lets a Saathi sell to a kabadiwala OR a dry-waste centre, so the receipt design must let DWCC operators, not only kabadiwalas, issue the receipts, and each receipt should carry the material code, state (S1/S2), grams and paise at price level L1. The core conclusions (no formal continuation order found; scheme visibly running; do not gate Saathi onboarding on the ID) survive, and the status is already 'partly', so the answer holds with these caveats.

verdicts.question: Would Hasiru Dala, Saahas, ITC WOW's centre operators or the Karnataka waste-pickers' union co-run kabadiwala and Saathi onboarding, or run a DWCC as a pilot yard, and on what terms do such NGOs usually work (fee per onboarding, grants, CSR)? What is Hasiru Dala Innovations' own traceable-plastic business with brands, and how should Luma.Green avoid competing with it?
verdicts.problems: Verification limits: no web source could be opened or searched in this session (WebSearch budget already exhausted at 200/200; fetches refused), so no claim is confirmed by a snippet; checks are internal consistency, cross-cluster comparison and the refined-chain files. Corroborated by independent repo passes: Hasiru Dala supports 35 DWCCs (its own 2024-25 report says 34 operator-run centres) and the registered Karnataka waste-pickers' union has 2,300+ members (Citizen Matters 15 Sep 2025, recorded by the personas and identity passes); the '11,300+ ID cards' sits consistently above the 10,437 Bengaluru cards via Hasiru Dala since 2011 (identity cluster) and 'over 10,000' (30 Stades, May 2021). (1) A contradiction with another pass: this answer states HDI has been 'supplying The Body Shop ... 250 tonnes in year one, 900 tonnes over three years, up to 2,500 Bengaluru waste pickers' as delivered fact, but the credits cluster records HDI's own blog ('The world's first ethically traded plastic', dated 30 Jul 2026, at hasirudalainnovations.com/blog-detail/3/...) as putting the HDI-PFC-Body Shop volume at 64 t PET; the 250/900 t figures are the 2019 launch commitments from Plastics for Change and should be labelled as commitments. The two clusters also cite that blog at different URL paths (/blog/... here vs /blog-detail/3/... there), so one path is likely wrong. (2) Missed development that changes the HDI relationship: BSWML's 2026 Authorised Waste Processor list names 'Sustainable Impacts with Hasirudala Innovations' as the AWP for the Bengaluru South corporation (BSWML user-fee declaration and bulk-waste page, Apr 2026, recorded in the swm-2026 cluster), so in South wards HDI is part of the city's authorised bulk-waste channel and a compliance gatekeeper, not only a competing buyer; the 'avoid competing' advice must account for that, and a pilot yard could subcontract under it. Likewise Saahas Zero Waste already runs rePurpose Global's 'Project Sada Shakti' plastic-credit project in Bengaluru (Oct 2024, credits cluster), so the same neutrality rule applies to SZW. (3) Figures found only in this cluster and confirmed by no other pass: Saahas (226 livelihoods, 5,227 MT, CSR partners) and SZW (420+ staff, 100+ t/day, 112 workers formalised, 10-TPD Jigani MRF, 25 t/month textile unit, three 'Let's Transform' micro-entrepreneurs with about 20 workers each), ITC WOW 2024-25 (17,900+ collectors, 150+ social entrepreneurs, 67,100 MT), HDI's Rs 5 crore FY2017-18 revenue and Social Alpha, 370+ clients, 800+ events, 327 supplier clients, Vishuddh Recycle, the Rs 50 membership fee, Swachha, Gilgal and Thyajya Shramika Sanghatane as named bodies; the ITC and company-page figures are from live pages dated 'accessed 29 Sep 2026' and can change. (4) The lapsed BBMP MoU amounts reused here carry the same unreconciled arithmetic flagged in the DWCC verdict. (5) Refined-chain conflict: 'run a DWCC as the pilot yard' mis-types the node; in the founder's model a Hasiru Dala DWCC is a 'Dry-waste centre / MRF' role (sorting facility, city-agreement holder) while HDI's aggregation centre is a Yard/Aggregator selling bales to pre-processors and recyclers (S3 out, L2/L3 prices), SZW's Jigani MRF is an MRF node and its textile unit a pre-processor; the per-onboarding and Rs 10,000 monthly fee benchmarks are reasonable as NAMASTE-derived defaults but remain open items, and since Luma.Green digitises the DWCC's legal records the fee may run the other way or be zero.
verdicts.correction: No public page commits any partner; each needs a meeting. Partner fit under the refined chain: Hasiru Dala (member-based, resource organisation for 34-35 Bengaluru DWCCs, 10,000-11,300+ ID cards secured, grant/CSR-funded) is the Saathi-onboarding partner and one of its centres is the pilot 'dry-waste centre / MRF' node (not the yard); Saahas Zero Waste's IKEA-funded 'Let's Transform' scrap-dealer programme is the closest template for kabadiwala onboarding (its figures are from its own pages and unconfirmed); ITC WOW is a CSR super-franchisee network to approach after the pilot; the registered Karnataka waste-pickers' union (2,300+ members) is the body to consult on Saathi pay. Fee defaults: benchmark a per-onboarding fee to NAMASTE's Rs 250 and any monthly centre-support fee to Rs 10,000 per DWCC, but treat both as open items — no NGO publishes a rate, and because Luma.Green keeps the DWCC's daily weight sheet and sale register, the arrangement may be a service exchange rather than a fee. Hasiru Dala Innovations is a separate for-profit running total waste management, EPR services and a WFTO fair-trade, traceable post-consumer plastics line that aggregates from waste-picker entrepreneurs, DWCCs and scrap dealers and sells to recyclers and brands; its Body Shop supply via Plastics for Change was launched on 9 May 2019 with commitments of 250 t in year one and 900 t over three years, while HDI's own 2026 blog cites 64 t PET — use the 64 t figure as the delivered volume and the rest as commitments. Two 2026 facts change the competition picture: HDI (with Sustainable Impacts) is BSWML's Authorised Waste Processor for the Bengaluru South corporation under the 2026 bulk-waste regime, so in South wards it is the legal route for bulk-generator dry waste and a possible umbrella for a pilot yard; and Saahas Zero Waste already hosts rePurpose Global's plastic-credit project. So Luma.Green should stay a neutral ledger that records cash/UPI sales and never buys, sells or brokers material, EPR certificates or plastic credits, model HDI's aggregation centre as a Yard/Aggregator node (S3 bales out at L2/L3) and SZW's Jigani MRF as an MRF node, and offer both a traceability export shaped for their WFTO, EPR and credit audits. Ask Hasiru Dala, SZW, HDI and the union directly; ask a CA about routing CSR money under Section 135 to a CSR-1 partner. Status: partly.
